prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, which opened a new regime of precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Having read the full first round, I find the case stronger on the points that matter to me as an experimentalist. The invention is specific: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift of the clock transition so that thousands of neutral atoms can be held without Doppler and recoil shifts, and the later realisation at JILA brought systematic uncertainty and stability to the 1e-18 level. The result is quantitative, and it has been reproduced and compared across independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL). It opened a door, in the sense I used in 2023 for attosecond physics: millimetre-scale relativistic redshift, tests of constant variation, geodesy with clocks and dark-matter searches were not measurable before. Five of eight members now hold this position with identical names and no one disputes that the measurements are real. I note that support counts are not my argument. The argument is that this is an original experimental invention with verified performance, and that the credit maps onto two people.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch, frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche, control of single quantum systems and ion clocks) remains the strongest objection, and I take the chair's question seriously. My answer is that those prizes honoured the comb as a ruler and the control of single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different physical system with a different enabling idea, the magic-wavelength condition, which allows ensemble interrogation by neutral atoms. If the citation names the lattice and the magic wavelength explicitly, it separates the work from both earlier prizes. The objection would become decisive for me only if the committee wanted to avoid any further prize in precision time and frequency metrology, and I do not think the statutes require that. Second, the SI second has not been redefined. I treat that as a consequence, not a precondition: the statutes ask for a discovery or invention that has been experimentally verified and that matters, and the clock comparisons already verify it. Waiting for a metrological body decision would make the prize depend on a procedural timeline unrelated to the physics. Third, the credit outside the pair: I cannot establish from the material before me that Lemonde, Pal'chikov or the ion-clock groups have a priority claim that is stronger than that of the people who built a working lattice clock, and I would want that checked against the primary record before a vote. Takamoto and Ludlow carried out the key experiments in the groups of Katori and Ye respectively, which in my reading is a reason to credit the group leaders, not to add names. Finally, my preference for B012 may partly reflect that I value instrument-driven advances; I have tried to test it against B042 on the same criteria and report that below.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B012 first, names the magic wavelength in her citation, and asks colleagues from other fields to test her view because she knows the area closely and may over-weight it. The chair also asked her and Kroll to say plainly whether Ye's place is justified.
responses.response: Your request is the right one, and I am not an atomic physicist, so I can test it from the outside. On the evidence in the record, the idea and first demonstration of the lattice clock are Katori's, and the performance that made it a new regime of measurement (1e-18 level uncertainty, clock stability, comparison of ensembles) is Ye's. If the citation were to read only 'for the invention', Ye's place would be harder to defend, which is why I prefer wording that includes development and the new precision regime. I would like you to say, from your knowledge, whether the many-body lattice clock and the strontium clock records are central or separate from the main line; if they are separate I would leave them out of the citation rather than add a third name. I also agree with your wording that names the magic wavelength, and have adopted it in my citation.

responses.point: Kroll supports the same pair and citation, but asks whether the first lattice-clock demonstrations and the many-body clock work should be described separately, and he asks how much a metrology prize can repeat a subfield after 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I would not describe the demonstrations separately in the citation. The concise wording 'invention and development' covers both the first lattice demonstrations and the record-accuracy realisation, and a longer citation would invite the credit disputes we are trying to avoid. On repeating a subfield, I think the right test is whether the work is a distinct original experiment, not whether the neighbourhood has been honoured before. The comb in 2005 and ion control in 2012 enabled optical clocks, but neither prize addressed trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and the committee has recognised several different advances within one broad area before. I accept your point that this is a judgment the committee must make explicitly, and I would state in discussion that the lattice, not metrology generally, is the topic.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers twisted bilayer graphene for its minimal model and high originality, concedes that its maturity and attribution are less clean, and says that a two-part prize with B012 is impractical under the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree that a two-part prize is impractical: B012 alone uses two names, and adding B042 would require four or more. Your own description of B042 is also the reason I stay with B012. You list four unsettled points: the earlier continuum-model work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, the first-author role of Cao, the follow-up groups, and the unsettled mechanism. For a prize for the original experiment, I need to be sure that I have identified the people who did it, and for B042 I cannot yet say that. I do not dispute the originality or the impact, and if the committee found a defensible experimental credit I would rank B042 as my second choice, as I did in round 1.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B042 as a prediction followed by a clear clue from nature, ranked B012 second, and lists the overlap with earlier prizes as the limit on its novelty.
responses.response: I appreciate that you rank B012 second and judge it acceptable. On the mechanism question the chair raised, I would treat it as a follow-up for the discovery of the correlated and superconducting states, which I regard as an observation in itself. My difficulty is credit rather than that: three names in B042 cover two theorists and one experimentalist, while the 2018 experiments were by a group in which the first author, Yuan Cao, would be excluded. If you can show me a credit split that the experimental record supports, I would take that seriously. Otherwise, given that you already name B012 as an alternative, I ask you to consider whether maturity and clean credit should decide between two valid discoveries.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B042, says that a more mature topic such as optical lattice clocks would be safer if timing or credit is not clean, and also notes that he chaired the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
responses.response: Your own statement that the lattice clock would be the safer choice if timing or credit is unclear is close to what I am arguing, and I think it reflects a real committee difference between a result that is settled and a field that is still moving. I also note your disclosure about 2025. It reinforces my view that B005 should not return to the discussion this year, which I said in reply to Johansson. I would invite you to say whether, if the committee cannot settle the credit for B042 this year, you would be content to vote B012, and what further evidence would let B042 be considered next year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the argument that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct invention and not an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; this is a judgment, not a fact I can verify.

Whether the primary record gives Lemonde, Pal'chikov or others a priority claim that I cannot check from the materials available, and whether the central contribution of Ye is development of the record clock only.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second will be read by others as a precondition; I treat it as a consequence.
For B042, whether an honest experimental credit can be found within three names, and whether the mechanism question is resolved enough by the next cycle.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted name. I disclosed in round 1 that Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, and that is unchanged; he has stated his own conflict on B005 and it does not affect B012, which is my preferred configuration. My long-standing exchanges with the microscopy communities in Tokyo, Tohoku and Kyushu do not involve Katori (RIKEN/University of Tokyo) in any research or financial way, but I mention the Tokyo link for completeness since he is a professor there. I have no tie to Ye or JILA.
